title: RBI in Cushing, Oklahoma: Crude Tank Farm Inspection Planning
description: Risk-based inspection for Cushing crude tank farms: floor, roof and foundation risk, the breakout tank boundary, Oklahoma rules and remote API 580 studies.
h1: Risk-based inspection for the Cushing crude storage hub
intro: Cushing is a hub of tanks rather than process units: large-diameter crude tanks, most with external floating roofs, joined by manifolds, pump stations and pipeline connections. This page is for the integrity, tank and inspection managers who look after them. It explains where risk actually sits in a Cushing crude tank, why the federal breakout tank rule decides how much a risk assessment may change, which Oklahoma and federal rules apply, how storms and earthquakes feed into the plan, and how Atlantis runs a remote RBI study for a tank farm, with US technicians available to collect the readings it needs.

highlights.p: Neighbouring tanks holding the same crude can corrode at very different rates because of water handling, sludge, mixer use, cathodic protection and foundation drainage. Each tank is assessed on its own records, so a farm-wide average never sets an individual tank's plan.

Whether a tank is a breakout tank on a pipeline system decides what a risk assessment is allowed to change. The study classifies every tank at the outset, with your compliance staff, so the plan never proposes an interval the federal rule would not accept.

The assessment runs remotely. Where shell readings are old, annular plates have never been measured or roof pontoons have no history, Atlantis can send UT, MT, PT and VT technicians to Cushing to collect the data and feed it back into the model.

sections.h: A storage hub built between pipelines
p: Cushing, in Payne County, is where dozens of crude pipelines meet, bringing oil from Oklahoma, the Permian, the Rockies and Canada and sending it on to Gulf Coast and Midwest refiners. It is the physical delivery point for the NYMEX WTI crude contract, and more than a dozen separate terminals ring the town. Storage there exists to hold crude between pipelines and between market positions, so the tank farms are dominated by large crude tanks, most with external floating roofs, operated by several midstream companies.

That purpose shapes the risk picture. Inventories swing with the market: EIA reported that Cushing crude stocks fell below 20 million barrels from mid-June to mid-July 2026, low enough for the agency to discuss whether some operators were nearing the minimum working levels sometimes called tank bottoms. Tanks that run near their low levels for months, or that sit full and quiet through a long storage play, experience different product-side conditions from tanks that turn over weekly, and the RBI model should know which pattern each tank has followed.

sections.h: Where the risk sits in a Cushing crude tank
p: A process-plant RBI study spreads attention across hundreds of vessels and circuits. A crude tank farm concentrates it in a handful of components that repeat tank after tank, and the bottom is almost always the largest contributor, because it cannot be seen in service and a leak goes straight into the ground. The table shows how the assessment breaks a tank down and what it needs for each part.

sections.h: Breakout tank or terminal tank: what the risk assessment may change
p: Many Cushing tanks are breakout tanks: tanks that relieve surges in a hazardous liquid pipeline system or that receive and store crude carried by pipeline for reinjection and onward transport. Federal pipeline rules require those tanks to be inspected to API 653 but exclude the standard's risk-based alternative for setting internal inspection intervals, so their internal intervals stay on measured floor corrosion rates and the minimum bottom thickness expected at the next inspection. A terminal tank that is not part of a pipeline system sits under EPA's oil spill prevention rule and Oklahoma's aboveground tank rules instead, and the risk-based option in API 653 remains available within its own conditions.

Whether a given tank answers to PHMSA, to the Oklahoma Corporation Commission's pipeline programme or to neither depends on how it is connected and operated, and the answer is not always the same for tanks in the same farm. The study therefore opens with a classification table, agreed with the people who own pipeline compliance at your company, and every later recommendation respects it.
None of this makes RBI pointless for breakout tanks. The risk ranking still decides where inspection effort goes inside the intervals the rule allows.

sections.h: Consequence: what a release from a crude tank means
p: Probability tells you which tanks are likely to leak; consequence tells you how much a leak would matter. For a crude tank the consequence side is dominated by the environment and by business interruption more than by people, although a floating roof fire or a large release inside a dike can endanger the workforce too. API RP 581's tank bottom consequence approach weighs the volume that could escape, how fast it is detected, the soil beneath the tank and the route to groundwater and surface water, and those inputs differ across a large farm.

Secondary containment matters as well: dike capacity, the condition of dike walls and floors, liners and the drainage valves that must be kept closed. On the business side, a tank that has to be emptied unexpectedly removes storage that shippers have contracted, and in an interconnected terminal one tank's outage can constrain the manifold and its neighbours. The assessment records those factors explicitly, so a high-consequence tank is visible as such even when its corrosion rate is modest.

sections.h: Floating roofs, storms and the Oklahoma climate
p: Oklahoma weather is hard on external floating roofs. Severe spring thunderstorms dump heavy rain that the roof drain has to carry away; hail damages seals and coatings; ice storms freeze drains and load roofs in winter; and summer heat drives evaporation and seal wear. On Cushing's floating-roof tanks, standing water or product on the deck, damaged seals and blocked roof drains are typical findings, and a sunken or tilted roof can take a tank out of service as surely as a floor leak.

Lightning is the other roof risk. Rim seal fires on floating-roof crude tanks are a known hazard, and API RP 545 sets out lightning protection practice for those tanks. An RBI plan for a Cushing farm therefore treats the roof as a system with its own inspection tasks, covering pontoons, deck plates, seals, shunts, drains and supports, rather than as a footnote to the floor, and names a severe storm as an event that triggers roof and drain checks before the tank's routine schedule comes round.

sections.h: Earthquakes and settlement on the tank pads
p: North-central Oklahoma saw a run of earthquakes over the last decade, including a magnitude 5.0 event near Cushing in November 2016, after which operators checked their tank farms. A large-diameter crude tank shaken by an earthquake can suffer settlement, damage at the shell-to-bottom joint, loads on nozzles from stiff connected piping and foundation cracking, and none of those show up in a corrosion-rate calculation.

The plan handles seismic events the same way it handles storms: as reassessment triggers with a defined list of checks. After a felt event above an agreed threshold, the list typically covers a visual walk of each tank, settlement readings at the established points, examination of the shell-to-bottom weld and the annular plate where the walk-down or survey suggests movement, and a look at nozzle and manifold connections. Settlement results are evaluated against the settlement annex of API 653 by the owner's inspector, and the outcome is written back into each tank's record.

sections.h: Oklahoma and federal rules at a Cushing terminal
p: The Oklahoma Corporation Commission regulates many aboveground storage tanks through its Petroleum Storage Tank Division under Title 165, Chapter 26 of the Oklahoma Administrative Code, which lists API 653 among its referenced standards and requires compliance with EPA's spill prevention rule; tanks used in oil and gas exploration and production are handled through the Commission's oil and gas programme instead. The Commission's Pipeline Safety Department oversees intrastate pipeline operators under its federal certification, while interstate hazardous liquid lines and their breakout tanks fall to PHMSA under 49 CFR Part 195. EPA's Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure rule expects integrity testing of aboveground oil containers to an industry standard, typically API 653 for field-erected tanks.

OSHA's process safety standard is a different question at a crude tank farm than at a refinery. The standard exempts flammable liquids stored in atmospheric tanks and kept below their normal boiling point without chilling or refrigeration, so atmospheric crude storage that is not connected to a covered process often falls outside it. Applicability depends on the site, and pressure vessels at pump stations may also come under the Oklahoma Department of Labor's boiler and pressure vessel programme. The RBI report notes which regime governs each item so that the plan can be checked against the right rule.

sections.h: How a remote RBI study for a Cushing tank farm runs
p: A tank farm study starts with the tank register and the inspection file for each tank, collected through a shared data room: diameter, height, construction year and design code, roof and bottom type, any replacement bottoms, linings and coatings, cathodic protection design and surveys, release prevention barriers and leak detection, previous internal and external inspection reports, floor scan maps with prove-up readings, shell thickness by course, settlement surveys and repair records. Service history matters as much as hardware, so we also ask for crude grades handled, water draw records, sludge removal, mixer operation and periods of low-level or idle storage.

The first workshop, held by video with your terminal operations, integrity and corrosion people, confirms the breakout tank classification and the consequence inputs for each tank. Damage mechanisms are assigned to API 571, probability and consequence are assessed at the level you choose, from a qualitative screen to API RP 581's tank methods or your company's own procedure, and each tank receives a plan: external inspection tasks, in-service shell readings, the next internal inspection date on the basis its classification allows, floor scan coverage and prove-up rules, and roof and drain checks. Workshops run in Central time, the same as Houston, and the results are returned in a form your inspection records system can load.

sections.h: Field data at Cushing, and who signs the plan
p: Tank records at an older hub are often uneven: some tanks have a full floor map from the last internal, others only a few spot readings; shell surveys were taken at different locations each time; annular plates were never measured; and roof pontoons have no inspection history at all. Your own inspectors or tank contractor normally close those gaps. Atlantis can also send UT, MT, PT and VT technicians to Cushing for shell thickness surveys at repeatable locations, annular plate and lower shell measurements, corrosion mapping on suspect areas, pontoon readings, visual examination of roofs and seals, and magnetic particle or penetrant examination of shell-to-bottom welds after repairs. Atlantis does not carry out radiography in the United States, so any radiographic examination is done by your licensed contractor.

The plan is a recommendation. Your API 653 inspector, or the operator's inspection authority, reviews it, sets the intervals that go into the schedule and signs the inspection reports; Atlantis does not act as inspector of record. If a floor or shell finding needs an engineering assessment beyond the code's acceptance rules, that fitness-for-service evaluation stays with your engineer and is not offered by Atlantis, and the tank's risk record is updated once the outcome is known.

faqs.q: Is RBI worth doing on a tank farm where many tanks are breakout tanks?
faqs.a: Yes, although it does a different job there. Internal intervals for breakout tanks stay on measured corrosion rates under the current federal rule, but the risk ranking still decides which tank comes out next, how much of each floor is scanned, how prove-up is targeted and what each tank receives between internals. It also builds the likelihood and consequence record that PHMSA's June 2026 proposal would require if it becomes final.

faqs.q: How does the study treat a tank that has never had a floor scan?
faqs.a: It uses what is known, such as age, bottom design, cathodic protection history, service, water handling and the floor condition of similar tanks, and records the missing data as a gap with a conservative assumption in its place. That usually raises the tank's probability of failure until real data exists, and the plan says what inspection would replace the assumption.

faqs.q: Can RBI change which tanks we take out of service each year?
faqs.a: It can inform that choice. When several tanks are close to their due dates, the ranking shows which carries the most risk, taking floor condition, consequence and roof issues into account, and the out-of-service sequence can follow it within the limits of the rules and your system's capacity. The final schedule is set by your inspector and operations team.

faqs.q: How should earthquakes be handled in the plan?
faqs.a: As reassessment triggers with a defined check list. After a felt event above an agreed threshold, tanks are walked, settlement is re-read at the established points and the shell-to-bottom joint, annular plate and nozzle connections are examined where movement is suspected. Results go to your API 653 inspector and back into each tank's record.

faqs.q: Does OSHA's process safety standard apply to our Cushing tank farm?
faqs.a: Often not, but it depends on the site. The standard exempts flammable liquids stored in atmospheric tanks kept below their normal boiling point without chilling or refrigeration, so stand-alone atmospheric crude storage is frequently outside it, while tanks connected to a covered process may be inside. The RBI report notes the governing regime for each item so the plan is checked against the correct rule.

faqs.q: Can the study include the manifold, transfer piping and pump station equipment?
faqs.a: Yes. Manifold and transfer piping can be added as circuits assessed to API 570 practice, with attention to dead legs, low points where water collects, soil-to-air interfaces and supports, and pressure vessels at pump stations can be included on the API 510 side. Pipeline segments regulated under Part 195 are listed separately because their integrity management follows its own rules.

faqs.q: Can Atlantis technicians work at Cushing?
faqs.a: Yes. Atlantis can send UT, MT, PT and VT technicians for shell surveys at repeatable locations, annular plate and lower shell readings, corrosion mapping, pontoon checks, roof and seal inspection and surface examination of repaired welds. They work under your terminal's safety and permit rules, and radiographic work is left to your licensed contractor.

faqs.q: Who sets the next internal inspection date?
faqs.a: Your API 653 inspector or the operator's inspection authority. For breakout tanks the date rests on measured corrosion rates under the current federal rule; for other tanks it may use the risk-based option in API 653 within its conditions. The study recommends a date and shows its basis, but it does not approve it.
